title: Service charge budgets
description: Why service charges go up, how a budget is set and how a reserve fund saves for big costs. We prepare service charge budgets for blocks and estates.

intro.heading: What a service charge budget does
paragraphs: The service charge is the money leaseholders pay, under their lease, towards running, repairing and insuring the building. The service charge budget is the plan for the year's spending. It sets how much each leaseholder pays.

Belgarum Property Management prepares the budget with whoever manages the building under the leases. That can be the freeholder (the owner of the building and the land), a resident management company (RMC) or a right to manage (RTM) company. A sound budget covers the year's costs and saves for large ones. That way, leaseholders are less likely to face sudden bills.

included.heading: What's included
items: Preparing the yearly service charge budget with the board or freeholder
Planning what goes into the reserve fund (savings for large future costs) each year
Splitting the budget between leaseholders, in the shares each lease sets out
Sending service charge demands to each leaseholder
Holding the money in a designated trust account for the block or estate, separate from our own money
Credit control by our own team, so the money the budget depends on comes in
Comparing spending against the budget, ready for the year end accounts

steps.title: Look back at the last year
steps.text: We compare last year's spending with its budget. This shows where costs went up or down, and why.

steps.title: Draft the new budget
steps.text: We set out the costs for the coming year, such as insurance, cleaning, gardening, repairs and our management fee. We add what the building needs to save in the reserve fund.

steps.title: Agree it with the board or freeholder
steps.text: We go through the draft with the board or freeholder. They agree the final budget.

steps.title: Send the demands
steps.text: We work out each leaseholder's share, as the lease sets out, and send the service charge demands. The money goes into the building's designated trust account.

steps.title: Track spending through the year
steps.text: Our accounts team records every cost against the budget. At the year end, this becomes the [service charge accounts](/services/service-charge-accounts).

proof: Our own accounts team keeps the books for each block or estate.
Our block accounts and bookkeeping specialist has been with us since 2014.
Each block or estate has its own designated trust account, named for that building.
Credit control is done in-house, with independent solicitors for arrears when needed.

faqs.question: Why has my service charge gone up?
answer: Usually because the building's costs have risen, or it needs to save more for future works. Insurance, energy, contracts and repairs are common causes.
Each budget line shows what the money is for, and your property manager can take you through it.

faqs.question: What is a reserve fund?
answer: A reserve fund is money collected and saved for large future costs, such as a new roof or external redecoration. It is sometimes called a sinking fund. Saving a little each year means a smaller bill when the work is due. Your lease sets out whether the building can hold a reserve fund.

faqs.question: What does the service charge pay for?
answer: It pays for running, repairing and insuring the building, as the lease sets out. Typical costs include insurance, cleaning, gardening, repairs and the management fee. It may also include a payment into the reserve fund.

faqs.question: Who decides the budget?
answer: The freeholder, RMC or RTM company that manages the building under the leases. We prepare the budget and advise on it. The board or freeholder agrees it.

faqs.question: What can I do if I think a service charge is unreasonable?
answer: The law says service charges must be reasonable. Start by asking your property manager to explain the charge. If you still disagree, you can take independent advice. A tribunal can decide whether a service charge is reasonable.
